cues.text: See the blue brain tissue here? When you feel a splitting headache, it feels like your actual brain is hurting.
But the brain itself has no pain receptors at all. Surgeons can even operate on it while patients are awake.
Now notice the red layers wrapped tightly around it.
The pain actually comes from the sensitive tissues, muscles, and blood vessels surrounding your brain and skull.
When triggers like stress, dehydration, or lack of sleep hit, these structures react.
Look at the left panel as the blood vessel widens.
Triggers cause the blood vessels in your head to swell or spasm, changing pressure inside.
This expansion irritates the nearby trigeminal nerve, the main pain pathway for the head and face.
Now follow those bright sparks up to the right.
The nerve fires distress signals rushing up to your brainstem, translating pressure into throbbing pain.
And that is why headaches are often your body's alarm system, reacting to stress, tension, or dehydration.
